common_name: Purple Back Alocasia (Reverse Alocasia, Checkered Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Divide rhizome offsets with at least one growth point in spring and pot into a chunky, well-aerated aroid mix; keep humidity high while new roots establish.

directions: Bornean jewel Alocasia with sagittate leaves marked in an irregular gray-green and dark forest-green mottled pattern, giving a marbled, camouflage-like checkering across the upper surface rather than the raised tile texture of Dragon Scale types. The name comes from the leaf underside, which is a saturated maroon-purple that contrasts sharply with the muted top color and shows through as a rim of purple along the wavy leaf margins. Growth is compact and clumping from a spreading rhizome, staying well under two feet, and new leaves often emerge tightly rolled and deep burgundy before unfurling to their mature coloring. Keep in bright, filtered light with high humidity and a fast-draining mix, since the thinner leaf substance is more prone to edge browning in dry air than thicker-leaved Alocasia species.

planting.note: Separate rooted rhizome sections in spring or early summer; this slow grower resents disturbance so handle roots gently and avoid repeated repotting.

directions: A Philippine species grown less for color than for silhouette: the thick, glossy, dark green leaves curl upward along both margins into a deep central channel, forming a distinct boat- or canoe-like trough instead of the flat, spreading blade typical of most Alocasia. Leaves are narrow and elongated relative to the genus, held more upright on comparatively short petioles, and the waxy surface gives them a rigid, almost succulent feel. It is a slow, rhizomatous grower that stays compact for years, making it well suited to a terrarium or tight collector shelf. Provide bright indirect light and consistent humidity; the tightly rolled leaf margins make standing water in the trough a rot risk, so avoid overhead watering and let the mix dry slightly at the surface between waterings.
sources: Marie Selby Botanical Gardens aroid collection notes

planting.note: Divide basal offsets from the rhizome once they carry independent roots; larger 'Grandis'-type trade specimens are usually sold as established divisions rather than propagated from seed.

directions: A Bornean understory species with deeply corrugated, bullate dark green leaves overlaid with contrasting ivory to pale-green primary veins that stand out sharply against the puckered surface. The sagittate leaf margins are finely toothed or wavy rather than smooth, a detail that helps separate it at a glance from smoother-margined jewel Alocasia. It is one of the parent species behind a number of larger-leaved collector hybrids, and plants sold under the trade name 'Grandis' represent a larger-growing selection of the same species rather than a distinct cultivar. Give it bright, filtered light, steady warmth, and high humidity; like most jewel-type Alocasia it is sensitive to soggy mix and benefits from a coarse, fast-draining aroid blend.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Alocasia species records

planting.note: Divide offsets at the base of the clump once they have their own root mass; often sold in trade under the older synonym Alocasia metallica or as Alocasia x mortfontanensis.

directions: A clumping, upright species whose narrow to moderately broad sagittate leaves carry a glossy bronze-to-purple metallic sheen distinct from the matte, near-black coloring of Alocasia infernalis already grown in the trade as Black Magic. The most reliable identifying feature is the petiole and stem, which are deep maroon-purple over their full length, and the leaf underside repeats that same purple-red tone beneath the bronzy top surface. This species has been used as a parent in several ruffled collector hybrids because of its saturated dark coloring and vigorous, freely offsetting growth habit. It prefers bright indirect light — too little light dulls the metallic cast to plain green — along with high humidity and a chunky, quick-draining aroid mix.

planting.note: Divide the freely produced basal offsets any time the clump is actively growing; this dwarf species multiplies quickly compared to most jewel Alocasia.

directions: A small, freely clumping species closely related to the already-listed Alocasia cucullata (Chinese Taro) but scaled down in every dimension, with glossy, mid-green, shield-shaped leaves where the petiole attaches well inside the leaf margin rather than at its edge. Individual leaves rarely exceed a few inches across, and the plant spreads by basal offsets into a dense, bushy mound rather than growing tall. Its compact size and tolerance of average indoor conditions make it more forgiving than most jewel Alocasia for a windowsill or small container. Provide bright, indirect light and a well-drained mix, allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings; it is more tolerant of brief cool spells than most Alocasia but still needs protection from frost.

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring; this is the wild-type species behind named selections such as 'Corazon' and 'Metallic Blue' already grown in cultivation.

directions: The straight species behind two named cultivars already grown in the trade, 'Corazon' and 'Metallic Blue,' both selected from this variable Philippine species — its Latin name, meaning 'differently leaved,' reflects how much leaf shape and color shift from one wild population to the next. Typical leaves are corrugated and heart-shaped to broadly sagittate, deep green with a network of paler, silvery-toned veins, and held on upright petioles from a clumping rhizome. Because of this natural variability, unselected seed-grown or wild-collected plants sold simply as Alocasia heterophylla can differ noticeably in vein contrast and leaf shape from either named cultivar. Grow in bright, filtered light with high humidity and a fast-draining aroid mix, and expect a dormancy-prone rest period with reduced leaf production during cooler, lower-light months.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Alocasia species records

planting.note: Divide offsets or rooted rhizome pieces after frost danger passes; this is the larger-growing wild-type species from which the compact cultivar 'Yucatan Princess' was selected.

directions: The wild-type Bornean species that gave rise to the compact, heavily puckered 'Yucatan Princess' selection already grown in cultivation, this straight species is considerably larger in every dimension, reaching several feet tall in warm, humid conditions with broad, glossy, deep-green sagittate leaves and comparatively flatter leaf surfaces than its dwarf cultivar. Paler venation traces the leaf's primary ribs against the darker blade, and mature clumps produce thick, upright petioles capable of supporting substantial leaf size. In frost-free climates it can be grown outdoors as a large-scale tropical accent; elsewhere it needs bright indirect light, high humidity, and a large container to reach its full stature. Give it more space and a richer, moisture-retentive but well-drained mix than smaller jewel Alocasia species require.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — tropical foliage for warm climates

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps or separate rooted suckers in spring; this Australian native tolerates cooler nights better than most tropical Alocasia.

directions: A rainforest-understory species native to the east coast of Australia, with large, glossy, bright-to-mid green heart-to-arrow-shaped leaves on thick, fleshy petioles arising from a spreading rhizome that colonizes shaded, moist ground over time. Unlike many showier collector Alocasia, its appeal lies in vigorous, reliable foliage and cooler-climate tolerance rather than leaf patterning, and it holds up to brief cool snaps better than most tropical Alocasia species. Historically the crushed stem and leaf sap were applied topically by Aboriginal Australians as a folk remedy for the sting of the related stinging tree (Dendrocnide), though the plant itself contains calcium oxalate crystals and is toxic if ingested. Grow in deep to partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil; it spreads readily in a bog garden or shaded border in frost-free to marginally frosty climates.
sources: Australian National Botanic Gardens — Alocasia brisbanensis species profile
